provenance.case: Mozilla Firefox rapid release (release train), from 2011

references.citation: Khomh, F., Dhaliwal, T., Zou, Y., Adams, B. (2012). Do faster releases improve software quality? An empirical case study of Mozilla Firefox. MSR 2012.

target.task: The City of Khulna runs an open data portal. Four staff publish datasets that nine city departments send in at irregular times, and users complain that they never know when new data will appear. Plan the portal's release process for 2027.

rules.text: cadence_weeks is the planned number of weeks between releases, a whole number from 2 to 13.
List 2 to 4 stages a dataset passes through before release.

target.format: Reply with JSON only, in this shape: {"cadence_weeks": 3, "if_dataset_not_ready": "...", "releases_in_2027": 8, "stages": ["..."]}, where if_dataset_not_ready is exactly one of the words ship_without_it or delay_release.

source_example.text: In 2011 Mozilla moved Firefox from a release every year or so to a rapid release cycle of six weeks. Firefox 5, shipped in June 2011, was the first version made under the new process. New code entered a channel called Nightly, moved after six weeks to Aurora, then to Beta, and finally to Release. Every six weeks each channel moved up one step, like carriages on a train that leaves on time. A feature that was not ready simply missed the train and waited for the next one, so the release date never moved. Release managers could still approve small, urgent fixes for a version already in Beta; these requests were called uplifts. The aim was to get finished work to users quickly and to make release dates predictable for users and add-on developers. Some enterprise customers complained that the fast pace left them no time to test, and Mozilla added an Extended Support Release in 2012. Google Chrome had used a six-week schedule since 2010; Firefox moved to a four-week cycle in 2020 and Chrome followed in 2021. Mozilla later replaced the Aurora channel with Developer Edition. The approach is now widely known as the release train model.

notes: The implied requirement is truly ambiguous on cadence because the source gives both six and four weeks; the check accepts both. The implied counter is ambiguous: 'half-empty releases' could also be fixed by a longer cadence while still shipping without late data. Stage names like Beta and Release are generic and are not checked. v2 migration notes: the format line no longer shows the placeholder 'ship_without_it or delay_release' as a value (models copied it literally); the allowed values are now given in words. Its cadence dummy changed from 6 to 3, because 6 is the source's cadence and the required value in requirement-stated-full, so a model that copied the format shape passed T1 there without using the example. Browser names and terms (I1 to I4) in a stage label are odd, not false, so they are UNCLEAR wherever no ban is stated (counter-stated-full gained one user sentence that states it); add-on developers (I5) do not exist for a city portal and stay MUST_NOT. In requirement-implied-full the cadence unit is MUST, not UNCLEAR: the unit covers both the six-week and the later four-week cadence and T1 accepts both. Counter T1 checks moved to must_not_transfer.
